# Summary: Richard Stallman
Richard Stallman, born in 1953 in New York City to a Jewish family, showed early interest in computers, beginning with reading IBM manuals as a pre-teen. He excelled academically at Harvard University, earning a physics degree magna cum laude in 1974, and subsequently joined MIT’s Artificial Intelligence Laboratory as a programmer and hacker. Stallman was deeply involved in software development projects such as TECO and Emacs and became an outspoken critic of proprietary software restrictions, especially condemning practices like password control and software time bombs in the late 1970s and early 1980s.
In 1983, Stallman initiated the GNU project, aiming to create a free Unix-compatible operating system, and founded the Free Software Foundation (FSF) in 1985 to support free software advocacy. He authored pivotal tools including GNU Emacs, GCC, and GDB, and popularized the concept of copyleft and the GNU General Public License (GPL). Stallman advocates for software freedom as a moral imperative rather than mere pragmatism, insisting on terminology emphasizing freedom (e.g., "free software" over "open source") and on naming the GNU/Linux operating system to highlight GNU’s contributions. His activism extends to opposing software patents, digital restrictions, and surveillance. After controversies over comments linked to the Jeffrey Epstein scandal, Stallman resigned from MIT and FSF leadership in 2019 but returned to the FSF board in 2021, amid mixed reactions from the free software community. He lives in Boston, identifies as an atheist, and continues to promote software freedom and privacy principles.
